title: The Next Big Chip Failure May Be A Security One
gist: A closed-door DAC roundtable of security leaders from Arteris, Cadence, Keysight, Rambus, Siemens EDA, Synaptics, and Synopsys argues chip security is shifting from an engineering afterthought to a board-level business requirement, driven by AI models (like Anthropic's Mythos) that can now find hardware-level vulnerabilities, and by regulation (EU Cyber Resilience Act) that attaches financial penalties to unpatched hardware trust failures that can persist for years, unlike software bugs.

themes.theme: Security must shift left into the design flow

insights.claim: Chip security leaders argue that starting the security conversation between security, design, and verification teams early in the design phase matters more right now than getting the technical solution perfectly right, because the target itself will keep shifting as technology evolves.
insights.speaker: Michal Siwinski, EVP, chief product and marketing officer, GM for security solutions at Arteris
insights.so_what: Signals that EDA/security IP vendors should productize 'early-stage security planning' tooling (requirements capture, cross-team workflows) as a near-term wedge, since most design teams reportedly lack this today.
insights.quote: It’s important to get going, even if you don’t get it right. If you’re not starting now, you’re too late.

insights.claim: Security cannot be 'glued on at the end' of chip design — companies that lack foundational security elements risk failing power/performance/area (PPA) targets, failing security certifications, and being forced into costly chip respins.
insights.speaker: Reed Hinkel, director of strategic programs for security, processor, wireless, and NVM at Synopsys
insights.so_what: Frames security-by-design as a direct cost-avoidance argument (avoiding a chip respin) rather than a compliance nicety — useful framing for security IP vendors selling into skeptical hardware teams focused on area/power budgets.
insights.quote: But if they don’t understand what their security target is in the beginning, and at least have a minimum viable baseline, they’re probably going to fail with their product in the long run.

insights.claim: Chip security is following the same historical adoption arc as automotive functional safety (ISO 26262): once a taboo topic companies avoided discussing, it has become a mandatory, regulation-and-customer-driven conversation with commercial upside (ability to market a product as 'safe'/'secure' raises ASP).
insights.speaker: Michal Siwinski, EVP at Arteris
insights.so_what: Provides an investable analogy: functional-safety IP and certification tooling became a durable revenue category after ISO 26262 matured; expect a similar multi-year build-out of security IP, verification, and certification tooling revenue as chip security regulation matures.
insights.quote: It went from something that used to be a taboo topic to something that became a reality. We have to deal with it, and here are best practices. Cybersecurity, at least in semiconductors, is going through exactly the same journey

insights.claim: Arm has recently gone public about restructuring how all of its processors are built to account for hardware security across the full software-to-hardware stack, after years of working on it privately.
insights.speaker: Michal Siwinski, EVP at Arteris
insights.so_what: A named, verifiable industry data point: Arm's public pivot on hardware security is a bellwether that IP licensees across the Arm ecosystem will need to follow suit, creating downstream demand for security verification tooling among Arm licensees.
insights.quote: Arm just went through this. Arm has been doing this for years. They just went public that they’re doing this a few weeks ago
insights.locator: Siwinski on Arm's public security pivot

themes.theme: AI as both attacker and scale multiplier

insights.claim: LLMs became capable in April (referencing the 'Mythos' event) of not only finding unknown software vulnerabilities but also propagating that vulnerability discovery down to the hardware/silicon level, making chip security no longer purely a software question.
insights.speaker: Michal Siwinski, EVP at Arteris
insights.so_what: Marks a discrete inflection point (April, Mythos) after which hardware vulnerability discovery is AI-accelerated — investors should track AI-driven security tooling vendors racing to keep pace with AI-driven attack discovery, since the article frames this as an arms race.
insights.quote: that’s when the LLMs, all of a sudden, were able to not only find new weaknesses, the unknown unknowns in software, but also get to the hardware level

insights.claim: Unlike software vulnerabilities that can typically be patched quickly once found, hardware vulnerabilities such as Spectre and Meltdown continue to have new variants reported weekly years after original disclosure, illustrating that hardware flaws are far harder to fully close.
insights.speaker: Michal Siwinski, EVP at Arteris
insights.so_what: Underscores that AI-discovered hardware vulnerabilities carry a much longer remediation tail than software CVEs — a structural reason hardware security spend should be viewed as a durable multi-year line item, not a one-time patch cycle.
insights.quote: in hardware we’re still dealing with Spectre and Meltdown. To this day, there are variants of that still happening and being reported weekly.

insights.claim: The security industry is fundamentally a scale problem: there are far too few people who understand root of trust and security, the space of exploitable weaknesses is unbounded, and 'good AI' (defensive) must outrace 'bad AI' (offensive) in a knowledge-democratization race that neither side is guaranteed to win.
insights.speaker: Chris Giles, director of product management for static and formal verification at Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: Frames chip security spend as an open-ended arms race rather than a solvable, bounded problem — supports continued, non-cyclical demand for both formal verification tooling and AI-driven security scanning as long as the offense/defense AI gap persists.
insights.quote: I don’t believe that the state space of secure and exploitable weaknesses is bounded. There’s something out there that is exploitable.

insights.claim: The best current industry approach to finding hardware vulnerabilities is essentially reactive — checking that previously exploited violation classes are not repeated — while acknowledging that unknown-unknown exploitable weaknesses remain undiscovered, a gap AI is now being applied to close (for both attackers and defenders).
insights.speaker: Chris Giles, director at Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: Implies current formal/static verification methodology is necessary but insufficient; vendors that can demonstrate AI-augmented discovery of novel (not just known-pattern) vulnerabilities have a differentiation opportunity over legacy checklist-based verification tools.
insights.quote: The problem is, it’s the stuff you don’t think of, even with specifications, even with people who really understand security. There is something out there.

themes.theme: LLM/agentic AI introduces new silicon-level attack surface

insights.claim: The primary security threat for LLMs running at the silicon and data-center level is not data privacy but 'integrated corruption' — an attacker tampering with a prompt or model weights to alter the model's execution path, since the model's data effectively defines what code executes.
insights.speaker: Yathiendra Vunnan, senior application engineer at Cadence
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI security investment thesis away from privacy-focused tooling and toward integrity/execution-path verification for models running on hardware — a distinct product category (weight/prompt integrity attestation) from typical data-privacy AI security tools.
insights.quote: Most people are focused on LLM data privacy, but at the silicon and data center level, we believe the major threat is on integrated corruption. Your data defines what you want to execute.

insights.claim: Because LLM vulnerabilities can recur (the same underlying weakness may resurface with similar future data even after a fix), there's no guarantee a previously exploited data-driven vulnerability in an agentic workflow stays fixed, raising open questions about agentic workflow security assurance.
insights.speaker: Yathiendra Vunnan, senior application engineer at Cadence
insights.so_what: Signals a gap in current tooling: continuous/ongoing verification of agentic AI workflow security (not one-time patching) is an unsolved problem space, worth watching for new security-verification product categories.
insights.quote: once you have a vulnerability, do you know if the next time you use a similar type of data that you actually have a guarantee the data is secure?

insights.claim: Companies shipping agentic co-pilot frameworks that rely on third-party frontier models face a new security challenge: securing the channel to an external party (the frontier-model provider) that sits inside their trust boundary, which some are mitigating by hosting their own LLMs on-premises or at the edge.
insights.speaker: Alexander Petr, senior director and portfolio manager at Keysight EDA
insights.so_what: On-prem/edge LLM deployment as a security mitigation is a concrete, actionable trend for hardware vendors — supports demand for edge inference silicon and on-prem AI infrastructure specifically driven by security/trust concerns, not just cost or latency.
insights.quote: In some cases we rely on frontier models, which are not owned by our companies
insights.locator: Petr on frontier model risk mitigation

themes.theme: Regulation turns security into a business-critical requirement

insights.claim: The EU's Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and the U.S. software security design framework (SSDF) are converting security compliance into direct financial liability for chip and software vendors, with the CRA explicitly threatening profit-based penalties.
insights.speaker: Alexander Petr, senior director at Keysight EDA
insights.so_what: Regulatory penalty exposure (CRA) is now a quantifiable business risk that should factor into valuation/risk models for chip and software vendors selling into the EU — creates durable demand for compliance-oriented security verification tooling.
insights.quote: The European CRA is even worse because they’re telling you that if you do something wrong, your profit is on the line and you’re going to pay penalties.

insights.claim: Security has moved from a purely engineering problem to primarily a business/trust problem, with the Cyber Resilience Act forcing companies to establish and maintain trust across a product's full lifecycle, not just prove security at launch.
insights.speaker: Mohit Arora, senior director of architecture at Synaptics
insights.so_what: Lifecycle-trust obligations (not just point-in-time certification) imply recurring revenue opportunities for vendors offering ongoing device attestation, patching infrastructure, and vulnerability-disclosure management rather than one-time security audits.
insights.quote: security moving from an engineering problem to mostly a business problem now
insights.locator: Arora on CRA and lifecycle trust

insights.claim: Denial-of-service is described as the most dangerous and easiest-to-execute attack type today, often used for extortion (cutting off vital system functions and demanding cryptocurrency payment), and many victims — outside of financial and certain mandated institutions — are not required to report breaches, which understates the true scale of the problem.
insights.speaker: Reed Hinkel, director of strategic programs at Synopsys
insights.so_what: Public breach statistics likely materially understate real-world attack incidence due to non-mandatory reporting outside finance — investors should discount official breach-count data and expect reporting-mandate expansion (a regulatory catalyst) to reveal a larger addressable security market than currently visible.
insights.quote: There are whole cities where water supplies have been held hostage, and there’s no good reporting system. You’re not mandated to report that you had the breach, which I think you should be.

insights.claim: The cost of mounting physical attacks against chips has collapsed with AI assistance — what previously required roughly a million-dollar attack budget can now be achieved far more cheaply, including via third-party labs offering attack services, removing physical-attack capability from being a nation-state-only threat.
insights.speaker: Mohit Arora, senior director of architecture at Synaptics
insights.so_what: A quantifiable cost-collapse data point (million-dollar to commodity-priced) for physical/hardware attacks — implies mid-market and consumer device makers, not just defense/aerospace, now face physical-attack-grade threats and should budget for tamper-resistant hardware accordingly.
insights.quote: the bar for physical attacks has gone very low, because with AI assistance, it’s so easy. What previously was supposed to be a million-dollar attack is no longer the case. It’s a much cheaper attack now.
insights.locator: Arora on collapsing physical attack costs

themes.theme: Hardware trust as the non-negotiable foundation

insights.claim: Secure services depend on secure software, which in turn depends on secure hardware underneath it — companies without a tamper-resistant hardware team or partner cannot achieve true 'ground truth' trust regardless of how much software-layer security they build.
insights.speaker: Scott Best, senior director for silicon security products at Rambus
insights.so_what: Positions tamper-resistant hardware IP as the non-substitutable base layer of the security stack — reinforces durable demand for silicon security IP vendors (Rambus, Synopsys) regardless of how much software/AI security tooling proliferates above it.
insights.quote: secure services do not work without secure software underneath it. Secure software doesn’t work unless there’s secure hardware underneath it. So coming from a hardware company, one of the things you need to get started is hardware security, because not all hardware is created equal.

insights.claim: Historically, hardware/system security practice concentrated on 'integrity' within the CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability), underweighting availability, even though availability failures are now the most dangerous and easiest attack vector, particularly for autonomous systems where loss of availability can be safety-critical.
insights.speaker: Reed Hinkel, director of strategic programs at Synopsys
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, historically underinvested security dimension (availability) that is now rising in priority due to autonomous systems — a potential product gap for security IP/monitoring vendors to fill relative to legacy confidentiality/integrity-focused tooling.
insights.quote: for many years, security was concentrated on a little bit of the I (integrity). People didn’t understand the importance of availability, which becomes incredibly important for two reasons. One, if you have autonomous systems, the functionality has to be available all the time.
insights.locator: Hinkel on CIA triad and availability

insights.claim: Complex modern SoCs can have roughly 200 power domains/nodes that are constantly transitioning, making it hard for a root of trust or security processor to maintain visibility, pushing security design from static permission-based models ('deny this, deny that') toward context-aware runtime monitoring (e.g., flagging why an NPU is accessing the Bluetooth stack's memory).
insights.speaker: Mohit Arora, senior director of architecture at Synaptics
insights.so_what: A concrete architectural complexity metric (~200 power nodes) that explains why static permission-based security models are becoming obsolete — supports demand for runtime, context-aware security monitoring IP over legacy static access-control schemes.
insights.quote: a more complex SoC could have like 200 power nodes. The chip is constantly being beaten down, going in and out of various domains.
insights.locator: Arora on 200 power nodes and context-aware security
